title: Presentation of benefits and harms of antidepressants on websites: A cross-sectional study
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of 39 consumer health websites from 10 countries, judged against 14 predefined evidence-based criteria. Several shares of websites carrying explicitly evidence-contradicted claims are reported with counts and denominators: 29/39 (74%) attributed depression to a chemical imbalance or claimed the drugs fix one, 23/25 (92%) of the sites mentioning suicidality contained incorrect information, 22/23 (96%) of those mentioning addiction stated SSRIs are not addictive, 13/28 (46%) of those covering withdrawal had misleading or incorrect information. These are truth/falsity judgements against an external evidence standard, so CONTENT applies. The composite “met our predefined standards” judgement is completeness-based and is recorded as QUALITY.

estimates.country: Australia, Canada, Denmark, Ireland, New Zealand, Norway, South Africa, Sweden, United Kingdom, United States
estimates.platform: Consumer health websites reached at the top of Google searches
estimates.measure_type: % of popular antidepressant/depression websites that attributed depression to a “chemical imbalance” or claimed antidepressants fix or correct such an imbalance, a claim the authors' criteria state has no evidence
estimates.value_raw: Twenty-nine (74%) websites attributed depression to a “chemical imbalance” or claimed they could fix or correct that imbalance
estimates.denominator: 39 websites (9 governmental, 15 advocacy, 15 consumer organisations) from 10 English- or Nordic-language countries, at least two per country, taken from the top of Google searches for “depression”, “antidepressants” or “depression therapy”
estimates.definition: Website stated that depression is caused by a chemical imbalance, or that antidepressants fix or correct such an imbalance, against predefined criterion 3: “No evidence for a chemical imbalance as a cause of depression, or for drugs fixing or correcting an imbalance of chemicals in the brain”
estimates.misinfo_def: No general definition of misinformation is given; falsity is defined criterion by criterion against the research literature, e.g. criterion 3: “No evidence for a chemical imbalance as a cause of depression, or for drugs ﬁxing or correcting an imbalance of chemicals in the brain”.
estimates.source_quote: Twenty-nine (74%) websites attributed depression to a “chemical imbalance” or claimed they could ﬁx or correct that imbalance. Examples of misleading claims are shown in Table 5.
estimates.page_loc: p. 57, Section 3.3 “Chemical imbalance”; Table 4 row “Chemical imbalance” 29 (74%); also in the Abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two authors assessed each site against a list of 14 predefined criteria drawn from the research literature (refs 12–40); one author took the English-language sites and the other the Nordic-language sites, with doubts resolved by discussion; no inter-rater reliability statistic is reported and no second coder checked each site
estimates.moderator_quote: We tried to mimic what most people would do when searching for information on the Internet and therefore chose easily accessible websites, which appeared at the top of a Google search. We searched the term depression and when this did not provide information about pharmacological therapy, we searched the terms antidepressants or depression therapy.
estimates.notes: This is the cleanest full-sample estimate in the paper: a single specific false claim, judged over all 39 sites. It is NOT a “% of websites containing any misinformation” figure; the paper never reports one. RoB caveat that bears on the coding rather than the arithmetic: the authors (Nordic Cochrane Centre / Institute for Scientific Freedom) are prominent critics of antidepressants, and the criteria encode contested positions (e.g. that the drugs are addictive, that the effect is below clinical relevance), so the ground truth is the authors' reading of the evidence rather than a neutral guideline.

estimates.country: Australia, Canada, Denmark, Ireland, New Zealand, Norway, South Africa, Sweden, United Kingdom, United States
estimates.platform: Consumer health websites reached at the top of Google searches
estimates.measure_type: % of the websites that mentioned suicidality which contained misleading or contradictory information about it
estimates.value_raw: Twenty-ﬁve (64%) websites mentioned that antidepressants may cause increased suicidal ideation, but 23 (92%) of them contained misleading or contradictory information related to this
estimates.denominator: the 25 of 39 websites (64%) that mentioned antidepressants may cause increased suicidal ideation
estimates.definition: Website's account of suicide risk was misleading or contradictory against predefined criterion 7 (“The drugs may increase the risk of suicidality, with no age limit”); the paper gives examples such as claiming the association “has not been proved”, claiming there is “no clear evidence of an increased risk … in adults of 18 years or over”, or restricting the risk to when treatment first starts (13 of the 25 websites)
estimates.misinfo_def: Criterion 7: “The drugs may increase the risk of suicidality, with no age limit”.
estimates.source_quote: Twenty-ﬁve (64%) websites mentioned that antidepressants may cause increased suicidal ideation, but 23 (92%) of them contained misleading or contradictory information related to this.
estimates.page_loc: p. 59, Section 3.7 “Suicidality”; also in the Abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same two-author assessment against the 14 predefined criteria; no reliability statistic
estimates.moderator_quote: Thirteen of the 25 websites that mentioned the suicidal risk in patients misstated that the risk only occurs “when they ﬁrst start to take antidepressants” or similar
estimates.notes: CONDITIONAL DENOMINATOR: 25 sites, not 39. The share of ALL 39 sites carrying misleading suicidality information is not stated and would be a computed 23/39, which R8 forbids, so it is not recorded. Do not pool this 92% with full-sample rates.

estimates.country: Australia, Canada, Denmark, Ireland, New Zealand, Norway, South Africa, Sweden, United Kingdom, United States
estimates.platform: Consumer health websites reached at the top of Google searches
estimates.measure_type: % of the websites that mentioned addiction which stated that SSRIs are not addictive, contrary to the authors' evidence criterion
estimates.value_raw: Twenty-three websites (59%) mentioned “addiction” with reference to antidepressants but 22 (96% of those) stated that SSRIs are not addictive
estimates.denominator: the 23 of 39 websites (59%) that mentioned “addiction” with reference to antidepressants
estimates.definition: Website stated that SSRIs are not addictive, against predefined criterion 8: “Objectively and subjectively, the drugs are addictive”
estimates.misinfo_def: Criterion 8: “Objectively and subjectively, the drugs are addictive”.
estimates.source_quote: Twenty-three websites (59%) mentioned “addiction” with reference to antidepressants but 22 (96% of those) stated that SSRIs are not addictive. The remaining 16 websites did not make any reference to addiction at all. Only one of the 39 websites (3%), from Norway, acknowledged the addictive eﬀects of antidepressants
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same two-author assessment against the 14 predefined criteria; no reliability statistic
estimates.moderator_quote: The withdrawal reactions to SSRIs are very similar to those for benzodiazepines, which are widely acknowledged for their addictive properties [30]. It is therefore contradictory to claim that SSRIs are not addictive
estimates.notes: CONDITIONAL DENOMINATOR (23 sites, not 39). Flagged borderline because whether SSRIs are “addictive” is a contested framing rather than a settled fact: the authors' criterion 8 asserts it, and mainstream guidance distinguishes physical dependence and withdrawal from addiction. An adjudicator may reasonably judge this an author-position row rather than a clean falsity judgement.

estimates.source_quote: Twenty-eight websites (72%) informed patients about the withdrawal eﬀects caused by sudden cessation of antidepressants but 13 of these (46%) had misleading or incorrect information.

estimates.moderator_quote: Twenty-eight websites (72%) informed patients about the withdrawal eﬀects caused by sudden cessation of antidepressants but 13 of these (46%) had misleading or incorrect information.
estimates.notes: CONDITIONAL DENOMINATOR (28 sites, not 39). 13/28 is stated verbatim with both numbers, so the value is exact.

estimates.country: Australia, Canada, Denmark, Ireland, New Zealand, Norway, South Africa, Sweden, United Kingdom, United States
estimates.platform: Consumer health websites reached at the top of Google searches
estimates.measure_type: % of websites meeting the authors' 14 predefined standards for scientific evidence and informed consent (0% met them, i.e. all 39 failed)
estimates.value_raw: None of the websites met our predeﬁned standards for scientiﬁc evidence (see Table 4) [Abstract: “None of the websites met our predeﬁned criteria”]
estimates.definition: Website satisfied all 14 predefined criteria covering effect size, relapse, chemical imbalance, functioning/quality of life, sexual function, emotional numbing, suicidality, addiction, withdrawal, foetal harms, duration of treatment, tapering, psychotherapy and off-label prescribing
estimates.misinfo_def: No general definition; the composite standard mixes accuracy criteria with coverage criteria.
estimates.source_quote: None of the websites met our predeﬁned standards for scientiﬁc evidence (see Table 4).
estimates.page_loc: p. 55, Results opening; Conclusions p. 63; Abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two authors against 14 predefined criteria and three informed-consent guidelines (Medical Board of Australia, NHMRC, Canadian Medical Protective Association); no reliability statistic
estimates.moderator_quote: Based on a list of 14 predeﬁned criteria, we assessed whether the information presented was trustworthy, given the available evidence (see Table 3)
estimates.notes: ADJUDICATOR: read the direction carefully. value_pct 0 is the share that MET the standards, taken verbatim from “None of the websites met our predefined standards”. The complement (all 39 failed) is deliberately not written as 100 because R8 bars computed complements. Coded QUALITY, not CONTENT, and excluded from prevalence: the composite standard is failed by omission as well as by false claims (a wholly accurate site that simply does not mention off-label prescribing or emotional numbing fails), so it carries no veracity claim about what the site said.

missed_or_uncertain: NOT extracted, with reasons. (1) Table 4's per-criterion counts are labelled “Number of websites passing our standards for scientific evidence and informed consent”, but the rows are actually counts of websites MENTIONING each item, and for some rows mentioning is a failure (chemical imbalance 29 = 74%) while for others it is a pass (psychotherapy 37 = 95%). The caption contradicts the body; only the rows whose direction the Results text makes explicit were used. (2) Coverage/omission shares that carry no falsity judgement: relapse claims 22 (56%), functioning/quality of life 2 (5%), sexual function 23 (59%), emotional numbing 5 (13%), foetal harms 13 (33%), duration of treatment 29 (74%), tapering 20 (52%), psychotherapy 37 (95%), off-label prescribing 14 (36%), suicidality mentioned 25 (64%), addiction mentioned 23 (59%), withdrawal mentioned 28 (72%), and “only two (5%) websites noted that the suicide risk is increased in people of all ages”. These record whether a topic was covered, not whether the content was false, so they are completeness measures; recording each as a QUALITY row would breach R4. (3) “Only one of the 39 websites (3%) … acknowledged the addictive effects”: the accurate-content complement of the addiction row, not itself a misinformation share. (4) “16 (80%) of these did not detail time frames” (of the 20 sites advising tapering): an incompleteness measure. (5) Funding composition (21 sites 54% not industry funded, 12 sites 31% industry funded, 6 sites 15% no response): a source attribute. (6) “An Australian study showed that 88% of people think it's the likely cause of depression”: a public-belief figure cited from another study, barred by R8 and outside the belief exclusion anyway. (7) Effectiveness claims quoted from individual sites (60–70%, 70%, 50–70% recovery) are the websites' own contested claims, not study estimates. JUDGEMENT CALL: the paper reports no overall “share of websites containing any misinformation”; the 74% chemical-imbalance row is the closest full-sample figure and should not be read as an any-misinformation rate.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis of 39 consumer-facing websites (9 governmental, 15 advocacy, 15 consumer organisations) from 10 English- or Nordic-speaking countries, at least two per country, selected as those appearing at the top of Google searches for “depression”, and where necessary “antidepressants” or “depression therapy”; sites aimed only at practitioners or requiring logins were excluded; pages archived and dated between April and August 2018. Assessment against 14 predefined criteria for scientific evidence plus three informed-consent guidelines. Division of labour rather than double coding: one researcher took the English-language sites and the other the Nordic-language sites, with doubts resolved by discussion; no inter-rater reliability statistic is reported. Funding status was chased by email or phone where unclear (6 sites never responded). No patient or public involvement. Stated limitation: the study is limited to sites ranking highly on Google in each country. Not stated but material: the evidence criteria are the authors' own contested positions on antidepressant efficacy, addictiveness and suicide risk, so the ground truth is not independent of the authors.
rob.item6_quote: Based on a list of 14 predeﬁned criteria, we assessed whether the information presented was trustworthy, given the available evidence (see Table 3) [12–40]. These criteria were either of obvious importance considering the research literature on antidepressants, or represented controversial issues, e.g. whether the drugs are safe during pregnancy, which is also important to know for the users.
rob.item10_quote: Twenty-nine (74%) websites attributed depression to a “chemical imbalance” or claimed they could ﬁx or correct that imbalance.
